chunks: "High-speed signals go on layers that sit directly next to a solid reference plane, preferably ground, and I try to keep each interface on one layer, or at most one layer pair, from end to end.
The cleanest choice is usually an inner stripline layer, with a ground plane on both sides.
The field is fully contained, so there's less radiation and crosstalk, and it's well shielded from outside noise.
For short links, like a USB pair from a connector to the chip, or for very fast signals where via stubs would hurt, I'd use the top layer as a microstrip over an unbroken ground plane.

What I avoid: routing a fast signal over a plane split or anti-pad slot, putting it next to another signal layer with no plane in between, or putting it next to a noisy power plane when I could use ground instead.
If it has to change layers, I use a transition between layers that share the same reference plane, or I put a ground via right beside the signal via so the return current can hop planes.
And for a differential pair or a bus, every member goes on the same layers with the same via count, so the delays match."
